question: What is @PathVariable in Spring MVC?
title: @PathVariable in Spring MVC — Extracting URL Path Segments
direct_answer: @PathVariable binds a value captured from a request-mapping URI template. For @GetMapping("/users/{id}"), a request to /users/42 binds id to 42 and Spring converts it to the declared parameter type. Path variables commonly identify resources, but route design—not the annotation—decides their business meaning.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of REST URL parameter extraction and how Spring MVC binds path segments to method parameters
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using @RequestParam for resource identifiers like user ID instead of @PathVariable, which breaks REST conventions and makes URLs look like /users?id=42 instead of /users/42
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the REST design principle that path variables represent resource identity (the 'what') while query params represent filtering or options (the 'how')

sections.title: Binding a URI Template Variable with @PathVariable
sections.content:
Path variables can also capture enums, UUIDs, dates with format configuration, or several nested identifiers. Encoded slash and matrix-variable behavior depends on path parsing/container settings and should not be assumed.

Use nouns and stable identifiers for resource routes as a common API convention, but do not state that every id must be a path variable. A collection search by external reference can validly use a query parameter.

sections.title: Quick revision
content: The template variable name must match the annotation/parameter name or be specified explicitly.
Type conversion failures normally produce a 400 response through MVC handling.
If the route pattern itself does not match, another mapping may handle it or the result is a no-handler/404 path.
Validate authorization and parent-child ownership separately from path binding.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: @GetMapping("/users/{id}") UserDto find(@PathVariable long id) binds /users/42. If the Java parameter name is unavailable or different, use @PathVariable("id"). A missing segment such as /users does not call this method because it is a different path pattern. An invalid long such as /users/abc reaches conversion failure if the route pattern otherwise matches.

sections.title: @PathVariable at a Glance
sections.content:
amber|@PathVariable|~From the URL path|/users/{id} to id|part of resource identity|required by default
blue|Binding|~Template to parameter|name must match {placeholder}|or @PathVariable("id")|type-converted automatically
emerald|Use for|~Identifying a resource|/orders/42|hierarchical paths|RESTful style
rose|Trap|~Missing path segment|/users/ with no id|gives 404, not null|path variables are mandatory

sections.title: Extracting User ID from URL Path
When to Use Path Variables
sections.content:
Use **@PathVariable** when the value represents a **resource identifier** or a mandatory part of the resource hierarchy. For example, `GET /users/{userId}` to retrieve a specific user, `DELETE /products/{productId}` to remove a product, or `GET /customers/{customerId}/invoices/{invoiceId}` for nested resources. Path variables are **required by default** — if the URL doesn't match the template, Spring returns 404.

Use them when the parameter is **not optional** and defines which resource you're operating on.

Avoid using them for filtering, sorting, or pagination — those belong in query parameters. A good rule: if removing the value makes the URL meaningless (like `/users/` with no ID), it should be a path variable.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Using @RequestParam for resource IDs**: Freshers often write `@GetMapping("/users")` with `@RequestParam Long id`, resulting in `/users?id=42` instead of the RESTful `/users/42`. This breaks REST conventions and makes URLs harder to read and cache.
- **Forgetting type conversion errors**: If a client sends `/users/abc` where `abc` can't convert to `Long`, Spring throws `MethodArgumentTypeMismatchException`. Freshers forget to handle this with `@ExceptionHandler` and return a proper 400 Bad Request.
- **Naming mismatches**: When the path variable name differs from the parameter name, you must specify it: `@PathVariable("userId") Long id`. Freshers forget the annotation parameter and get binding errors.

What happens if the path variable cannot be converted to the parameter type?

speakable_v2.hook: @PathVariable turns the dynamic parts of your URL into Java method parameters — no manual string parsing needed.

beats.label: what_it_is
beats.content: @PathVariable extracts a value embedded in the URL path itself. You define a template in your mapping annotation with curly braces — like /users/{id} — and Spring takes whatever is at that position in the actual request URL and injects it into the annotated parameter.

beats.label: why_it_exists
beats.content: Spring also handles type conversion automatically. If your parameter is Long, Spring converts the String segment to a Long. If it can't convert — like someone sends /users/abc and you expect a number — Spring returns 400 Bad Request.

beats.label: parts_or_states
content: Single variable: /users/{id} with @PathVariable Long id.
Multiple variables: /users/{userId}/orders/{orderId} with two @PathVariable parameters.
Name mismatch: if the URL template uses a hyphen like {product-id}, use @PathVariable("product-id") Long productId.
Regex constraint: /users/{id:[0-9]+} restricts the segment to digits only.

beats.label: pitfalls
beats.content: candidates miss: The parameter name in your Java method must match the template variable name exactly, unless you specify the name explicitly in the annotation. A mismatch causes a 500 error at runtime, not a compile-time warning.

speakable_v2.cap: REST convention: use @PathVariable for resource identity — the thing that says which specific resource. Use @RequestParam for options and filters.

question: What is @RequestParam in Spring MVC and when do you use it?
title: @RequestParam in Spring MVC — Query String Parameter Binding
direct_answer: @RequestParam binds request parameters, commonly from the query string, to a handler argument. It is required by default unless a default value, Optional, or required=false changes that contract. Use query parameters for filters, search, sorting, pagination, and other request options; they can also appear in form-encoded requests.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of query string parameter binding, which is essential for building list and search endpoints in real applications
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Making all @RequestParam fields required without default values, causing 400 errors when clients omit optional filtering parameters
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Show a realistic pagination or filtering example with required=false and defaultValue, demonstrating understanding of optional API design

sections.title: Binding Query Parameters with @RequestParam
sections.content:
Query parameters are not always optional and path variables are not the only mandatory inputs. For example, a required version or signature can be a request parameter by protocol design. The path/query distinction is about URI structure and semantics, not a hard required/optional rule.

Cap page size and collection parameter counts. Bind values into database queries rather than concatenating them, and document how repeated parameters are interpreted.

sections.title: Quick revision
content: GET /users?status=ACTIVE&page=0 binds status and page.
defaultValue supplies a fallback and makes the parameter non-required.
required=false with a primitive is awkward because a missing primitive cannot be null.
Spring conversion binds numbers, enums, collections, and custom types when converters exist.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: @RequestParam(defaultValue = "0") int page and @RequestParam(required = false) Status status provide a usable default page and optional filter. If a required parameter is missing, MVC normally raises MissingServletRequestParameterException. If a supplied number is malformed, conversion fails. A default should reflect the endpoint contract, not be added only to avoid errors.

sections.title: @RequestParam at a Glance
sections.content:
amber|@RequestParam|~From the query string|/users?status=ACTIVE|after the question mark|filters + pagination
blue|Options|~required + defaultValue|required=false for optional|defaultValue for a fallback|avoids missing-param errors
emerald|Use for|~Optional inputs|search, sort, page/size|not resource identity|key=value pairs
rose|Trap|~Required param missing|400 Bad Request|set required=false|or provide defaultValue

sections.title: User Search with Filtering and Pagination
When to Use Request Parameters
sections.content:
Use **@RequestParam** for **optional filtering, sorting, and pagination** in list endpoints. For example, `GET /products?category=books&minPrice=10&maxPrice=50` lets clients filter products without requiring a different endpoint for each filter combination.

Use it for **search queries** like `GET /users/search?email=john@example.com`.

Use it for **configuration options** that modify behavior, like `GET /reports?format=PDF&includeCharts=true`. Query parameters are perfect when the value is **optional or has a sensible default**. For pagination, always use `defaultValue` so clients can call `GET /users` without specifying `page=0&size=20` every time.

Avoid using query params for **resource identifiers** — that's what path variables are for. If the parameter fundamentally changes which resource you're accessing, it belongs in the path, not the query string.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Making all params required**: Freshers write `@RequestParam String status` without `required=false`, so clients must always provide every parameter or get a 400 error. This breaks flexibility — optional filters should be optional. Use `required=false` or `defaultValue` to avoid this.
- **Forgetting type conversion errors**: If a client sends `page=abc` and your parameter is `int`, Spring throws `MethodArgumentTypeMismatchException`. Freshers don't handle this with an exception handler, returning a confusing 500 instead of a clear 400.
- **Not using defaultValue for pagination**: Writing `@RequestParam int page` without a default means clients must always specify page numbers. Use `defaultValue="0"` so `GET /users` works without query params and still returns the first page.

speakable_v2.hook: @RequestParam is how you read the ?key=value pairs from the URL — the filtering and pagination parameters every list endpoint needs.

beats.label: what_it_is
beats.content: @RequestParam binds query string parameters to method parameters. These are the key-value pairs after the question mark in the URL — like /users?status=ACTIVE&page=0&size=10.

beats.label: why_it_exists
beats.content: By default, every @RequestParam is required. If the client doesn't include it, Spring returns 400. For optional parameters, you have two options: set required=false to get null when the parameter is absent, or provide a defaultValue to get a fallback.

beats.label: parts_or_states
content: defaultValue: use a string default when the param is absent — also implicitly makes the param optional.
required=false: Spring injects null. Use Integer not int — primitives can't hold null.
Map<String, String>: inject all query params at once, useful when you don't know the keys upfront.
Also works for HTML form submissions with application/x-www-form-urlencoded content type.

beats.label: pitfalls
beats.content: non-obvious: If you use required=false with a primitive type like int, Spring throws a NullPointerException when the parameter is absent because it tries to unbox null to int. Always use the wrapper type Integer when making numeric params optional.

speakable_v2.cap: The standard pagination pattern: @RequestParam(defaultValue='0') int page, @RequestParam(defaultValue='20') int size. Clients can omit them and get sensible defaults.

question: What is the difference between @PathVariable and @RequestParam?
title: @PathVariable vs @RequestParam — URL Path vs Query String
direct_answer: @PathVariable reads a named segment captured by a URI template, while @RequestParam reads a request parameter such as a query-string value. Resource identifiers often belong in paths and collection filters/options often belong in query parameters, but required versus optional is configured independently. Neither annotation provides authorization or validates resource ownership.

interviewer_intent.testing: REST API design understanding — this is a classic comparison question that reveals whether a candidate knows RESTful URL conventions
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using @RequestParam for resource IDs that should be @PathVariable, resulting in non-RESTful URLs like /users?id=42 instead of /users/42
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Articulate the REST design principle: path for nouns and resource identity, query for adjectives and filtering or modification

sections.title: @PathVariable and @RequestParam
sections.content:
Spring performs type conversion for both annotations. Conversion failures usually become 400-level errors; an unmatched path may become 404 through the application's no-handler flow. These outcomes can be customized.

Keep URLs stable and avoid exposing database implementation details as resource structure. Choose paths for identity/hierarchy and query parameters for operations over a resource/collection when that makes the contract easiest to understand.

**Example.** GET /users/42 uses @PathVariable long id because 42 identifies the resource. GET /users?status=ACTIVE&page=0 uses @RequestParam values because status and page modify the collection query.

sections.title: Quick revision
content: /users/42 -> @PathVariable id=42.
/users?status=ACTIVE -> @RequestParam status=ACTIVE.
A missing route segment means the route does not match; a missing required request parameter produces a request-binding error.
Use the public resource model rather than a slogan such as path=noun and query=adjective.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
Use /orders/900 when 900 identifies the order resource. Use /orders?status=PAID&sort=createdAt for a filtered collection. A lookup endpoint /orders?externalRef=ABC can still use a required query parameter when that is the search contract. A nested /users/42/orders/900 route still needs code to verify that order 900 belongs to user 42 and that the caller may see it.

For example, /orders/42 maps 42 with @PathVariable to one order, while /orders?status=PAID maps status with @RequestParam to an optional filter over the order collection.

sections.title: @PathVariable vs @RequestParam
sections.content:
amber|@PathVariable|~Resource identity|/users/42|part of the path|usually required
blue|@RequestParam|~Filter / option|/users?status=ACTIVE|query string|often optional
emerald|Rule of thumb|~Path = which resource|query = how to filter it|/orders/9?expand=items|combine both freely
rose|Trap|~Swapping them|filters in path = ugly URLs|ids in query = non-RESTful|pick by meaning

sections.title: @PathVariable vs @RequestParam in Code
When to Use Each Annotation
sections.content:
Use **@PathVariable** when the value **identifies a specific resource** or represents a mandatory part of the resource hierarchy. Examples: `GET /users/{userId}` to fetch one user, `DELETE /products/{productId}` to remove a product, `GET /departments/{deptId}/employees/{empId}` for nested resources. If removing the value makes the URL incomplete or meaningless, it's a path variable.

Use **@RequestParam** when the value is an **optional filter, sorting rule, or pagination parameter**. Examples: `GET /users?status=ACTIVE&role=ADMIN` to filter users, `GET /products?sort=price&order=DESC` to sort results, `GET /orders?page=2&size=20` for pagination. If the parameter refines or modifies the result set but doesn't change which resource you're addressing, it's a query param. A practical rule: path variables are for **navigating to a resource**, query params are for **customizing the response**.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Using @RequestParam for IDs**: Freshers write `@GetMapping("/users") getUserById(@RequestParam Long id)`, resulting in `/users?id=42`. This breaks REST conventions. Resource IDs should be in the path: `/users/42` with `@PathVariable`.
- **Mixing them incorrectly**: Using path variables for filters like `/users/ACTIVE/ADMIN` instead of `/users?status=ACTIVE&role=ADMIN`. Path variables force a rigid hierarchy; query params give flexibility.
- **Not understanding required defaults**: Both annotations require parameters by default, but the failure mode differs — missing path variables return 404, missing query params return 400. Freshers don't anticipate this when designing APIs that should accept optional filters.

followup_questions: When would you use @PathVariable for something other than an ID?
How do you design a REST URL for a nested resource (user's orders)?
Can you use both @PathVariable and @RequestParam in the same endpoint?

speakable_v2.hook: @PathVariable and @RequestParam both get data from the URL — but they live in completely different parts of it.

beats.label: what_each_is
beats.content: @PathVariable reads from the URL path itself — the segments before any question mark. You define the position using curly braces in the mapping template, like /users/{id}. The value is part of the resource address.

beats.label: what_each_is
beats.content: @RequestParam reads from the query string — everything after the question mark. Like /users?status=ACTIVE&page=0. These are modifiers: how to filter, sort, or paginate the result.

beats.label: when_to_pick
beats.content: Use @PathVariable when you're identifying a specific resource: GET /users/42 means user 42 specifically. Use @RequestParam when you're describing criteria: GET /users?status=ACTIVE means all active users. A single endpoint can use both — GET /users/{id}/orders?status=PENDING gets pending orders for a specific user.

beats.label: tiny_example
beats.content: gotcha: /users?id=42 works technically but breaks REST conventions. Interviewers notice this. Resource IDs belong in the path, not the query string.

speakable_v2.cap: Path for nouns, query for adjectives. The path identifies the resource; the query string describes how you want it.

question: How do you make @RequestParam optional with a default value?
title: Optional @RequestParam with defaultValue in Spring MVC
direct_answer: Set required=false when absence should be represented as null for a nullable/reference type, use Optional<T> when explicit absence helps, or provide defaultValue when the endpoint has a real fallback. A default value implicitly makes @RequestParam non-required. Prefer a default for primitive parameters because primitives cannot represent null.

interviewer_intent.testing: Practical API design knowledge — understanding how to build flexible endpoints that don't force clients to provide every parameter
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not setting defaults for pagination parameters, forcing clients to always specify page and size instead of having sensible defaults like page=0 and size=20
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Show a complete pagination example with defaultValue for both page and size, demonstrating production-ready API design

sections.title: Optional Request Parameters and Defaults
sections.content:
The default is text and goes through Spring's conversion service to the target type. An empty request parameter may also trigger the default under RequestParam semantics, which should be tested if empty and absent must differ.

Keep API defaults documented and consistent with pagination metadata. Cap size on the server rather than trusting a client-provided number.

**Example.** @RequestParam(defaultValue = "0") int page makes /orders use page 0 and /orders?page=2 use page 2. A default value also makes the parameter non-required; use Optional or nullable handling when absence has a distinct meaning.

sections.title: Quick revision
content: @RequestParam(required=false) String status -> null when absent.
@RequestParam(defaultValue="0") int page -> zero when absent or empty under Spring's rules.
Optional<T> distinguishes absence without a nullable parameter.
Validate bounds such as non-negative page and maximum size.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
A list endpoint can use @RequestParam(defaultValue = "0") int page and @RequestParam(defaultValue = "20") int size. A truly optional search term can use Optional<String> query or required=false String query. Do not invent a default status if absence is supposed to mean all statuses. Invalid supplied values still fail conversion or validation; defaultValue is not error recovery.

For example, @RequestParam(defaultValue = "20") int size gives /orders a size of 20 while /orders?size=50 supplies 50. I still validate an upper bound so a client cannot request an unbounded result.

sections.title: Making @RequestParam Optional
sections.content:
amber|required=false|~Makes it optional|null if absent|no 400 error|handle null yourself
blue|defaultValue|~Fallback value|implies required=false|"0" for page|"10" for size
emerald|Optional<T>|~Type-safe absence|Optional<String> param|no null checks|cleaner code
rose|Trap|~Primitive + missing|int with no value|throws on null|use Integer or defaultValue

sections.title: Optional Filters and Pagination with Defaults
When to Use Optional Parameters
sections.content:
Use **`required=false`** when the parameter is a **truly optional filter** with no sensible default. For example, `@RequestParam(required=false) String email` in a user search — if not provided, you search all users; if provided, you filter by email. The parameter being `null` is meaningful: it means "don't filter by this field." Use **`defaultValue`** when the parameter has a **sensible default value** that makes the API work without client input. This is the pattern for **pagination** (`page=0`, `size=20`), **sorting** (`sortBy="id"`, `order="ASC"`), and **boolean flags** (`includeInactive=false`). Default values make your API **easier to use** — clients can call `GET /users` and get the first 20 users without specifying `?page=0&size=20`.

Avoid making **search or filter strings** have default values like `defaultValue=""` — an empty string is different from `null` and might cause unexpected behavior in your repository layer.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **No defaults for pagination**: Freshers write `@RequestParam int page, @RequestParam int size` without `defaultValue`, forcing clients to always specify pagination. This makes simple requests like `GET /users` fail with 400. Always provide defaults for page (usually `0`) and size (usually `10` or `20`).
- **Using empty string as default**: Writing `@RequestParam(defaultValue="") String name` means `name` is never `null`, it's an empty string when omitted. This can break repository queries that check `if (name != null)`. Use `required=false` instead and handle `null` explicitly.
- **Primitive types with required=false**: Writing `@RequestParam(required=false) int page` doesn't work — primitives can't be `null`. Spring will throw an error if the parameter is missing. Use `Integer` (boxed type) instead: `@RequestParam(required=false) Integer page`, or use `defaultValue` with the primitive type.

seo.metaDescription: Learn how to make @RequestParam optional in Spring MVC — required=false, defaultValue, Integer vs int, and pagination best practices.

speakable_v2.standard_example: Spring Boot 3.2 REST API serving a mobile client
speakable_v2.hook: Making query parameters optional is how you build APIs that work with and without those parameters — defaultValue is the clean way.

beats.label: what_it_is
beats.content: There are two ways to make a @RequestParam optional. Set required=false and Spring injects null when the parameter is absent. Or set defaultValue with a string value and Spring uses that as the fallback.

beats.label: why_it_exists
beats.content: defaultValue is usually the cleaner choice because it means you never have to check for null in your method body. The parameter always has a value — either from the client or from the default. Pagination especially benefits from this.

beats.label: parts_or_states
content: defaultValue='0': page parameter defaults to the first page if not supplied.
required=false with Integer: nameFilter is null when absent — check before using.
Optional<String>: Java Optional works too — Optional.empty() when the parameter is absent.
Both approaches make the parameter optional — the difference is null vs a default value.

beats.label: pitfalls
beats.content: sharp edge: defaultValue is always a String, even if your parameter type is int or Long. Spring converts it. But if your defaultValue string can't be parsed to the parameter type — like defaultValue='none' for an int parameter — you'll get a TypeMismatchException at request time, not startup.

speakable_v2.cap: Validate the size parameter with @Max to prevent clients from requesting thousands of records in one call — ?size=99999 is a real attack vector.

question: What is @RequestParam with a List type in Spring MVC?
title: @RequestParam List — Multi-Value Query Parameters in Spring
direct_answer: @RequestParam List<String> ids can collect repeated values such as /items?ids=1&ids=2&ids=3. With Spring's normal conversion service, comma-delimited input can also be converted for suitable collection element types, but conversion rules/custom converters can change this. The parameter is required by default; use defaultValue, Optional, or required=false when absence has a defined meaning.

interviewer_intent.testing: Knowledge of multi-value query parameter binding in Spring MVC — shows understanding beyond single-value parameters
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not knowing @RequestParam can bind to List or array — Learners try to manually parse a comma-separated string
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Demonstrate both repeated parameter style and comma-separated style with actual code examples showing the difference

sections.title: Binding Repeated Query Parameters to a List
sections.content:
Do not manually split a String unless the public contract is deliberately one comma-encoded value and escaping rules are defined. Repeated parameters avoid ambiguity when a value itself can contain a comma.

For a destructive bulk operation, a JSON request body may be clearer than a very long query string, and DELETE request-body support can vary across clients/proxies. Choose the HTTP contract first; collection binding is only the MVC mechanism.

sections.title: Quick revision
content: Repeated keys are the clearest portable multi-value query form.
Element conversion can bind List<Long>, List<UUID>, and other supported types.
Validate collection size and each element.
A missing list, an empty list, and an invalid value are distinct API cases.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: @GetMapping("/items") List<ItemDto> find(@RequestParam List<Long> ids) binds /items?ids=10&ids=20. Spring converts each text value to Long and returns 400 when conversion fails. If the filter is optional, use required=false or Optional<List<Long>> and decide whether absence means all items or no filter. Limit the number of ids so one request cannot create an unbounded SQL IN list.

sections.title: @RequestParam with List
sections.content:
amber|List binding|~Repeated parameter|?ids=1&ids=2&ids=3|maps to List<String>|multi-select filters
blue|Comma form|~Single value split|?ids=1,2,3|also binds to a List|Spring splits on comma
emerald|Use for|~Bulk filters|tags, categories|batch lookups|/items?ids=...
rose|Trap|~Empty parameter|?ids= with no value|empty or [""]|set required=false

sections.title: Multi-Value Parameter Binding Examples
When to Use List-Type Request Parameters
sections.content:
Use `List<T>` parameters for **bulk operations** where clients need to select or filter by multiple values: `/api/orders?status=PENDING&status=PROCESSING` to fetch orders in multiple states. It's essential for **batch endpoints** like deleting multiple items: `DELETE /api/items?ids=1&ids=2&ids=3`.

Use it for **multi-select filters** in search or reporting endpoints: `/api/sales?regions=North&regions=South&regions=East` where users can pick multiple regions. For **tag-based filtering**, List parameters are natural: `/api/articles?tags=java&tags=spring&tags=rest`. If you need **unique values only**, use `Set<String>` instead of `List<String>` — Spring will automatically deduplicate. For **primitive types**, use boxed types (`List<Long>` not `List<long>`) because Spring's type conversion works with wrapper classes.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Manually parsing comma-separated strings**: Freshers often declare `@RequestParam String ids` then split it with `ids.split(",")`. Spring can bind to List directly — no manual parsing needed. Just use `@RequestParam List<String> ids` and it handles both repeated params and comma-separated values.
- **Using primitive arrays**: Writing `@RequestParam long[] ids` causes type conversion issues. Use boxed types: `@RequestParam List<Long> ids` or `@RequestParam Long[] ids`. Spring's conversion works better with wrapper classes.
- **Forgetting required=false for optional lists**: If the parameter is optional, you must set `@RequestParam(required = false) List<String> categories`, otherwise Spring throws an exception when the param is missing. Then check for null or empty in your code before using the list.

followup_questions: What is the difference between repeated params and comma-separated params in URLs?
How do you handle an empty list when @RequestParam List is required=false?

seo.metaDescription: Learn how to bind multi-value query parameters to List with @RequestParam in Spring MVC — repeated params, comma-separated values, type conversion.

speakable_v2.standard_example: Spring Boot 3.2 REST API serving a mobile client
speakable_v2.hook: When a client needs to pass multiple values for the same parameter, @RequestParam with a List handles it in one line.

beats.label: what_it_is
beats.content: Declaring @RequestParam with a List type lets clients pass the same parameter name multiple times. If a client sends ?ids=1&ids=2&ids=3, Spring collects all three values into the List automatically and converts each element to the right type.

beats.label: why_it_exists
beats.content: This is the clean way to handle batch lookups — like fetching multiple items by ID in a single request. Without it, you'd receive a single string with all values and have to split it manually.

beats.label: parts_or_states
content: List<Long> ids: Spring collects all ?ids values and converts each to Long.
String[] ids: arrays work too — same behavior.
required=false with a List: returns an empty list when the parameter is absent.
Spring 5 and later also auto-splits comma-separated values like ?tags=java,spring into a list.

beats.label: pitfalls
beats.content: production trap: An unguarded List<Long> ids with no size limit means a client can send ?ids=1&ids=2&ids=3... for thousands of IDs in one request. Validate the list size or set a maximum to prevent oversized queries from hitting your database.

speakable_v2.cap: For multi-select filters — like filtering by multiple statuses — @RequestParam List<String> statuses with ?status=ACTIVE&status=PENDING is the idiomatic Spring approach.

question: How do you design RESTful URLs with path variables?
title: RESTful URL Design with Path Variables — Best Practices
direct_answer: Resource-oriented paths usually use nouns, stable identifiers, and HTTP methods for protocol actions. Nest paths when the child is meaningfully scoped by its parent, but do not mirror every database relationship or assume nesting improves security. Authorization must verify ownership regardless of URL shape, and deeply nested paths can become brittle.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of REST principles and URL design conventions — shows thinking beyond just Spring annotations
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using verbs in URLs like /getUser or /deleteOrder — REST uses HTTP methods for actions, not URL verbs
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Show the complete CRUD URL design for a resource hierarchy with proper HTTP methods and nested resources

sections.title: Designing Resource-oriented Paths
sections.content:
Actions that are not natural CRUD can be modeled as subresources or state transitions, for example POST /orders/42/cancellations, rather than forcing every verb into a path. Consistency and documented semantics matter more than a slogan that URLs can never contain an action word.

Keep paths shallow enough to remain stable when domain relationships change. Use URI building utilities so context paths and proxy prefixes are handled correctly.

sections.title: Quick revision
content: Use /users/{userId} for one user and /users for the collection.
Use /users/{userId}/orders when orders are viewed in that user's scope.
A globally identified order can also use /orders/{orderId}.
Paths identify resources; query parameters commonly filter/sort collections; authorization is separate.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: GET /users/42 reads a user representation; DELETE /users/42 requests deletion. GET /users/42/orders lists that user's orders. GET /orders/900 may be clearer for an order with a global id. Including both user and order ids does not prove order 900 belongs to user 42; the service must verify that relationship and the caller's permission.

sections.title: RESTful URL Design Rules
sections.content:
amber|Nouns not verbs|~Resources, not actions|/users not /getUsers|HTTP verb = the action|GET/POST/PUT/DELETE
blue|Hierarchy|~Nest related resources|/users/{id}/orders|path = identity|keep it shallow
emerald|Plurals + lowercase|~Consistent naming|/orders/{id}|hyphens for words|/order-items
rose|Trap|~Verbs in the path|/createUser|/deleteOrder|breaks REST conventions

sections.title: RESTful User Resource with Full CRUD Operations
When to Use Path Variables for Resource Design
sections.content:
Use path variables when identifying a **specific resource instance** in a collection: `/products/{productId}` to get product 42.

Use **hierarchical paths** when modeling ownership or parent-child relationships: `/customers/{customerId}/invoices/{invoiceId}` shows that invoice 789 belongs to customer 123. For **filtering or searching** across multiple resources, use query parameters instead: `/products?category=electronics&minPrice=100`. Path variables are for identity, query params are for filtering. In RESTful APIs, path structure should mirror your domain model's relationships. If users own orders, and orders contain items, your URLs reflect that: `/users/{userId}/orders/{orderId}/items/{itemId}`. This makes the API self-documenting and intuitive for client developers.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Using verbs in URLs**: Writing `/createUser` or `/getOrderDetails` violates REST principles. The HTTP method is the verb — use `POST /users` and `GET /orders/{id}` instead. Freshers often copy SOAP or RPC patterns where actions are in the URL.
- **Mixing path variables with verbs**: Creating URLs like `/users/{userId}/delete` when it should be `DELETE /users/{userId}`. The HTTP method already expresses the action.
- **Flat URLs for hierarchical data**: Using `/orders/{orderId}` when orders belong to users. The URL `/users/{userId}/orders/{orderId}` better expresses the domain relationship and allows proper access control checks (does this order belong to this user?).

seo.metaTitle: RESTful URL Design with Path Variables | Spring Java Interview
seo.metaDescription: Learn REST URL design best practices — nouns not verbs, hierarchical resources, nested path variables, plural nouns, and HTTP method conventions.

speakable_v2.standard_example: Spring Boot 3.2 REST API serving a mobile client
speakable_v2.hook: RESTful URL design has a simple core rule: nouns in the path, verbs in the HTTP method. That one rule eliminates most bad URL patterns.

beats.label: what_it_is
beats.content: RESTful URL design uses the URL to identify a resource and the HTTP method to express the action. The path tells you what you're operating on. GET, POST, PUT, PATCH, and DELETE tell you what you're doing to it.

beats.label: parts_or_states
content: GET /users — list all users.
POST /users — create a new user.
GET /users/{id} — get one user.
PUT /users/{id} — replace a user.
DELETE /users/{id} — remove a user.
GET /users/{userId}/orders — list a user's orders.

beats.label: why_it_exists
beats.content: Use plural nouns: /users not /user. Use lowercase and hyphens for multi-word paths: /user-profiles not /userProfiles. Query parameters are for filtering and pagination — /users?status=active — not for defining a different resource.

beats.label: pitfalls
beats.content: candidates miss: /getUser, /deleteOrder, /createProduct are all anti-patterns. They put the action in the URL instead of the HTTP method. Interviewers from companies with public APIs — Amazon, Microsoft — specifically test this because it's a signal of REST maturity.

speakable_v2.cap: Keep nesting to two levels maximum. /users/{id}/orders is clean. /users/{uId}/orders/{oId}/items/{iId}/details is not — flatten it.
